question: Before hanging a unit of packed red cells, which of the following identification steps best prevents an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction?

answers.text: Check the patient's name on the wristband matches the blood bag label and ask a colleague to confirm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Checking the wristband alone is insufficient; the patient must actively verify their own identity to ensure the correct unit is given to the right person.

answers.text: Ask the patient to state their full name and date of birth, then cross-check against the blood compatibility label, wristband and request form

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. 'Positive identification' requires the patient to state their own identity. Cross-checking the stated name and DOB against the compatibility label, wristband and request form constitutes the complete bedside check.

answers.text: Confirm the ABO group printed on the blood bag matches the patient's last recorded group in the notes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Historic group records can be incomplete or erroneous; the formal bedside identity check against the current crossmatch label is required every time.

answers.text: Use the barcode scanner on the ward computer as the sole verification step

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Electronic verification is a useful adjunct but does not replace the direct verbal patient-identification step required by transfusion safety protocols.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the bedside positive-identification procedure required before every unit of blood is transfused.
Well done. Having the patient state their own name and date of birth, matched against the compatibility label, is the single most effective bedside safety check.
